newsitem.title: USA: Oil prices fall as worries ease on supply, weather.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices fall as worries ease on supply, weather.

text.p: NEW YORK (Chicago) - Oil prices fell Tuesday as traders focused on an expected rise in weekly inventories and ignored concerns that possible frigid weather would raise demand for heating oil in the Northeast.
In other markets, cold Midwestern weather boosted corn prices but wheat and soybean prices fell.
Heating oil for January delivery fell 1.28 cents to 73.54 cents a gallon at the New York Mercantile Exchange, giving back almost half the gains posted a day earlier.
Prices had jumped on Monday on forecasts that by the weekend a blast of Arctic air would hit the Northeast, the largest heating oil market in the world.
Snowstorms and bitter cold winds as chilly as 40 degrees below zero Fahrenheit continued to pummel the north-central United States Tuesday.
But Weather Services Corp. and other forecasters said the cold weather expected to hit the East Coast will not be as bitter as conditions seen in the Midwest.
"The profit-taking is to be expected after yesterday's move," said Dale Wong, trader with Nationsbanc-CRT in Houston.
Traders said they also expected the American Petroleum Institute to show a buildup of 500,000 barrels or more in U.S. distillate stocks in weekly data due on Tuesday afternoon.
Distillates consist of heating oil and diesel fuels.

After the close of trading, API reporting an increase in distillate stocks of 1.05 million barrels to 123.22 million in the week ended on December 13. But API also reported a drop of 2.20 million barrels in crude oil stocks and declines in both gasoline stocks and production in the week.
January crude oil fell three cents to $25.71 a barrel and January gasoline rose 0.25 cent to 69.77 cents a gallon before the release of the weekly API data.
Weather and supply-demand also played the key roles in grain trading.
Good growing weather for competing South American soybeans pushed down prices and cold Midwest weather aided corn, where demand for livestock feeding increases as temperatures fall.
January soybeans fell five cents to $7.06-1/2 a bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade. December corn rose 3/4 cent to $2.70-3/4 a bushel.
December wheat fell 9-1/4 cents to $4.04-1/2 a bushel after deliveries of an unexpectedly large 460,000 bushels of wheat were posted against the contract overnight.
Lack of a mill or an exporter of those deliveries diluted bullish sentiment about domestic demand for wheat, prompting a wave of speculative selling that pushed prices lower, traders said.
"There were new deliveries last night" that hurt prices, said Skip Searcy, wheat trading specialist for FIMAT Futures.

The wheat market has been buoyed recently by perceptions that U.S. domestic mills have been buying wheat in the futures market by accepting posted deliveries on the December contract. The contract is slated to expire on Thursday.
